short: A loan from an investor to a government or company, which promises regular interest and return of the original amount on a set date.
kid: You lend your friend ten sweets. Every week she gives you one extra sweet as a thank-you, and at the end of the month she gives all ten back.
detail: A bond is a tradable debt instrument: the issuer borrows a fixed sum, the face value, and promises to pay interest, called the coupon, at set intervals and to repay the face value at maturity. Governments issue bonds to fund deficits, and companies issue them as an alternative to bank loans. Bondholders are creditors, not owners, so they get no vote, but they are paid before shareholders if the issuer fails. After issue, bonds trade in the secondary market, and their prices move with interest rates and the issuer's creditworthiness. In India, government bonds trade mainly on the RBI's NDS-OM platform, while corporate bonds are listed on NSE and BSE. A common confusion is thinking a bond's return is just its coupon: if you buy at a price above or below face value, your actual return, the yield, differs from the coupon rate.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues a 5-year bond with a face value of ₹1,000 and an 8% annual coupon. A holder receives ₹80 a year for five years, ₹400 in total, plus the ₹1,000 back at maturity, for total receipts of ₹1,400.
formula: Bond price = C/(1+y) + C/(1+y)^2 + ... + (C + F)/(1+y)^n, where C is the coupon, F the face value, y the yield per period and n the number of periods

short: Investments, mainly bonds, that pay a set schedule of interest and return the original amount at a known date.
kid: Imagine a helper who promises to give you two sweets every Sunday, no more and no less. You always know what is coming, so you can plan your week.
detail: Fixed income is the asset class of investments whose cash flows are set in advance by contract: bonds, debentures, treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit and, broadly, bank fixed deposits. The investor lends money and receives scheduled interest plus repayment of principal. Because payments are known, fixed income is used for steady income, capital preservation and matching future liabilities, which is why pension funds, insurers and banks hold large amounts. In India, banks, insurers and debt mutual funds are the major holders of government and corporate bonds. The common confusion is that fixed means riskless: the cash flows are fixed, but the market price of a bond rises and falls with interest rates, and a company issuer can still default. Floating-rate and inflation-indexed bonds also count as fixed income even though their coupons change.
example: An investor puts ₹10 lakh into a 3-year bond paying 7% a year. She receives ₹70,000 each year, ₹2.1 lakh in total, and gets her ₹10 lakh back at maturity, provided she holds it to the end and the issuer pays.

short: The fixed interest a bond pays its holder, stated as a yearly percentage of the bond's face value.
kid: You lend your toy car to a friend. Each week she gives you a sticker for letting her play with it, and that sticker is your little reward.
detail: The coupon rate is the annual interest rate a bond pays on its face value, fixed when the bond is issued; the coupon payment is the cash amount actually paid. The name dates from paper bonds that had detachable coupons the holder clipped and presented for payment. Coupons may be paid annually, semi-annually, as with Indian government securities and US Treasuries, or quarterly, and some bonds have floating coupons reset against a benchmark rate. Issuers set the coupon close to prevailing market yields for their credit quality at the time of issue. The key confusion is treating the coupon rate as the investor's return. The coupon is based on face value, not on the price you pay, so if you buy a bond below or above face value, your yield differs from the coupon rate.
example: A ₹1,000 face value bond with a 7.5% coupon paid semi-annually pays ₹37.50 every six months, or ₹75 a year. That stays ₹75 whether the bond trades at ₹950 or ₹1,050 in the market.
formula: Annual coupon payment = Coupon rate × Face value

short: The amount a bond issuer promises to repay at maturity, on which the bond's coupon interest is calculated.
kid: When you lend a friend ten marbles, ten is the number she must give back at the end, however many she plays with in between.
detail: Face value, also called par or nominal value, is the principal amount stated on a bond. It is what the issuer repays at maturity and the base on which coupon payments are calculated. Indian government security prices are quoted per ₹100 of face value, US Treasuries per $100, and listed Indian corporate bonds come in face values that vary by issue, commonly ₹1,000 for public issues and higher for private placements. After issue, a bond's market price can move above face value, a premium, or below it, a discount, but the face value itself does not change. The common confusion is mixing up face value with price: a bond quoted at 98.50 costs ₹98.50 per ₹100 of face value, yet the holder still receives ₹100 at maturity. The face value of a share is a separate, purely accounting idea.
example: Say you buy a ₹1,000 face value bond of ABC Ltd for ₹960 with a 6% coupon. You receive ₹60 a year in interest, calculated on ₹1,000 not on ₹960, and ₹1,000 at maturity, a ₹40 gain over your purchase price.

short: The date on which a bond ends and the issuer must repay its face value; also the time remaining until that date.
kid: When you lend a friend your bicycle, you agree on the day she gives it back. That day is when the lending ends.
detail: Maturity is the date a bond's final principal payment falls due, after which no more coupons are paid. The term also describes a length of time: original maturity, or tenor, is the life of the bond at issue, while residual maturity is the time left from today. Instruments of a year or less, such as treasury bills and commercial paper, belong to the money market; longer ones are bonds. The Indian government has issued securities with maturities as long as 50 years, and the 10-year bond is the main benchmark. Longer maturity usually means larger price swings when interest rates change and, typically, a higher yield to compensate. A common confusion is equating maturity with duration: a 10-year coupon bond's duration is shorter than 10 years because part of the cash comes back earlier as coupons.
example: A government bond issued in April 2020 with a 10-year tenor matures in April 2030. Looked at in April 2026, its original maturity is 10 years and its residual maturity is 4 years.

short: The annual return an investor earns on a bond at its current market price, expressed as a percentage.
kid: If you lend sweets and get extra sweets back, the extras are your reward. Comparing the reward with what you gave tells you how good the deal is.
detail: Bond yield is the return a bond offers relative to its price. In news it almost always means yield to maturity, the single annual rate that equates the bond's price with its future coupons and principal. Yields move inversely to prices: when buyers pay more for a bond, its fixed coupons are a smaller return on the money invested. Benchmark yields, such as India's 10-year government security yield or the 10-year US Treasury yield, act as the risk-free reference for home loans, corporate borrowing costs and equity valuations, so a jump in them tightens financial conditions. They respond to expected central bank policy, inflation, government borrowing and foreign flows. For live levels, check the rates board rather than any fixed number. A common confusion is mixing yield with coupon: the coupon is fixed at issue, while the yield changes every day the bond trades.
example: A 10-year bond with ₹100 face value and a 7% annual coupon trades at ₹100, so its yield is 7%. If its price falls to ₹95, a buyer still gets ₹7 a year plus ₹100 at maturity, so the yield rises to about 7.74%.

short: The single annual return you earn if you buy a bond at today's price, hold it to maturity and every payment arrives as promised.
kid: Imagine paying for a box that hands you a sweet every week and a big cake at the end. Adding up everything you get, compared with what you paid, shows how good the box really is.
detail: Yield to maturity is the discount rate that makes the present value of a bond's remaining coupons and principal equal to its current market price, quoted as an annual rate. It is the bond market's standard measure of return because it combines coupon income with any gain or loss from buying below or above face value. It has no closed-form solution and is found by trial and error or a spreadsheet's YIELD or IRR function. YTM assumes the bond is held to maturity, the issuer pays in full and on time, and every coupon is reinvested at the same YTM, which rarely happens exactly. Indian government securities and US Treasuries pay semi-annual coupons, so their quoted YTM is the semi-annual rate doubled. A common confusion: YTM is the promised yield at today's price, not a guaranteed return if you sell early.
example: A 3-year bond with ₹1,000 face value and a 6% annual coupon trades at ₹973.76. Its YTM is 7%, because ₹60/1.07 + ₹60/1.07^2 + ₹1,060/1.07^3 = ₹56.07 + ₹52.41 + ₹865.28 = ₹973.76.
formula: Price = C/(1+YTM) + C/(1+YTM)^2 + ... + (C + F)/(1+YTM)^n, solved for YTM

short: A bond's yearly coupon payment divided by its current market price, showing its income return and ignoring any gain or loss at maturity.
kid: If a hen costs you ten coins and lays eggs worth one coin each year, you get one coin back for every ten you paid, just from the eggs.
detail: Current yield measures the income a bond pays relative to what it costs today: annual coupon divided by market price. It is quick to compute and useful for investors who care about cash income, such as retirees comparing bonds with fixed deposits or dividend-paying shares. Its weakness is that it ignores the pull to par, the gain or loss as the price moves towards face value at maturity, and the timing of cash flows. So for a bond bought at a discount, current yield is below yield to maturity, and for a bond bought at a premium it is above. Only for a bond priced exactly at par do the coupon rate, current yield and yield to maturity coincide. The common mistake is quoting current yield as a bond's total return.
example: A ₹1,000 face value bond with an 8% coupon pays ₹80 a year. At a price of ₹1,000 its current yield is 8%; at ₹800 it is ₹80 / ₹800 = 10%; at ₹1,250 it is ₹80 / ₹1,250 = 6.4%.
formula: Current yield = Annual coupon payment / Current market price

short: The annual return on a callable bond if the issuer repays it early, on the call date and at the call price.
kid: You lend a friend ten sweets for a month, but she is allowed to give them back after one week. You count your reward as if she gives them back early, since she might.
detail: Yield to call applies the yield to maturity calculation to a callable bond, but uses a call date in place of the maturity date and the call price, which may include a small premium over face value, in place of the face value. Issuers tend to call bonds when interest rates have fallen, because they can refinance more cheaply, and that is exactly when the bond trades at a premium. So for premium callable bonds, YTC is usually lower than YTM and is the more realistic estimate of return. Investors compute YTC for every possible call date; the lowest of these and the YTM is the yield to worst. A common confusion is assuming the call will happen: YTC is one scenario, not a forecast, and the issuer decides.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹1,000 bond with a 9% annual coupon and 10 years to maturity, callable at ₹1,000 in 2 years, trading at ₹1,050. If called, a buyer gets ₹90 and then ₹1,090, a YTC of about 6.26%, against a YTM of about 8.25% if it is never called.
formula: Price = C/(1+YTC) + ... + (C + Call price)/(1+YTC)^k, where k is the number of periods to the call date

short: The lowest yield a bond can deliver without default, checking every date on which the issuer is allowed to repay it early.
kid: Your friend may give back your borrowed toys on Monday, Wednesday or Friday. You plan for the day that gives you the least fun, so you are never disappointed.
detail: Yield to worst is the minimum of a bond's yield to maturity and its yields to every possible call date, and to other early-redemption dates such as sinking-fund dates. It assumes the issuer acts in its own interest, redeeming whenever that is cheapest for it, which is worst for the holder. YTW is the conservative yield quoted for callable bonds and is widely reported for corporate bond indices and funds, since many US corporate and municipal bonds have call features. It does not account for default: a bond's YTW can be high precisely because markets doubt it will be paid. The common confusion is reading YTW as a worst-case return; it is the worst outcome among the issuer's redemption choices, assuming no default and coupons reinvested at that same yield.
example: Say ABC Ltd's 9% bond trades at ₹1,050, with a YTM of about 8.25%, a yield to its 2-year call of about 6.26% and a yield to its 5-year call of about 7.76%. Its yield to worst is the lowest of these, about 6.26%.
formula: Yield to worst = Lowest of (Yield to maturity, Yield to each possible call date)

aliases: Inverse relationship between bond prices and yields
Bond prices fall when yields rise
hl: inverse relationship between bond prices and yields
short: The rule that when market interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall, and when rates fall, existing bond prices rise.
kid: If your swing gives one sweet per ride and a new swing gives two, nobody will pay much to ride yours. When new swings give fewer sweets, everyone wants yours again.
detail: A bond's coupons and principal are fixed, so its price is the present value of those cash flows at the market's current yield. If yields rise, the same cash flows are discounted at a higher rate and the price falls; if yields fall, the price rises. Economically, no one will pay full price for an old 6% bond when new bonds pay 7%, so its price drops until it offers a comparable return. The relationship is not a straight line: prices rise more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount, which is convexity. Longer maturities and lower coupons make prices more sensitive. The common confusion in headlines: rising yields mean falling bond prices, so a bond rally means yields are going down.
example: A 10-year ₹1,000 bond with a 7% annual coupon is priced at ₹1,000 when yields are 7%. If yields rise to 8%, its price falls to about ₹932.90; if yields fall to 6%, it rises to about ₹1,073.60.
formula: Price = Sum of [Cash flow at time t / (1 + y)^t], so a higher yield y gives a lower price

short: A bond trading at a price above its face value, usually because its coupon is higher than current market yields.
kid: If your toy gives out more sweets than newer toys, friends will happily give you more than you paid to get it. It is worth extra because it is so generous.
detail: A bond trades at a premium when its price exceeds face value. This happens when its coupon rate is above the yield the market now demands for similar bonds, typically because interest rates have fallen since issue or the issuer's credit has improved. The buyer pays extra upfront for the higher coupons, and that extra is gradually lost as the price drifts down to face value at maturity, so yield to maturity is below both the coupon rate and the current yield. Callable premium bonds carry added risk, because the issuer is likely to redeem early at a lower call price. A common confusion is thinking a premium bond is a better investment: the higher coupon is offset by the premium paid. In the UK, Premium Bonds are something else, a government savings product with prize draws.
example: A ₹1,000 bond with a 9% annual coupon and 5 years left is priced at a 7% yield. Its price is about ₹1,082, an ₹82 premium, which the holder gives up gradually as the price falls to ₹1,000 at maturity.
formula: Premium = Market price - Face value (positive when coupon rate > yield to maturity)

short: A bond trading at a price below its face value, usually because its coupon is lower than current market yields.
kid: If your toy gives out fewer sweets than newer toys, friends will only take it if they pay less for it. Getting it cheaply makes up for the smaller treats.
detail: A bond trades at a discount when its price is below face value. This happens when its coupon is lower than yields on comparable new bonds, typically because interest rates have risen since issue, or because investors now see more risk that the issuer will not pay. The buyer receives smaller coupons but gains as the price rises towards face value at maturity, so yield to maturity is above both the coupon rate and the current yield. Zero-coupon bonds and treasury bills normally trade at a discount because they pay no coupon, unless yields turn negative. A deep discount can signal distress: a corporate bond at half its face value suggests investors doubt full repayment. The common confusion is assuming a discount bond is a bargain; the low price usually just reflects a lower coupon or higher risk.
example: A ₹1,000 bond with a 6% annual coupon and 5 years left is priced at an 8% yield. Its price is about ₹920.15, a ₹79.85 discount that the holder earns back as the price rises to ₹1,000 by maturity.
formula: Discount = Face value - Market price (positive when coupon rate < yield to maturity)

short: A measure of how much a bond's price changes when interest rates move, also read as the average time to receive its cash flows.
kid: Shake a long skipping rope and the far end swings a lot; shake a short one and it barely wiggles. Some promises are like the long rope and swing a lot when things change; others are like the short one.
detail: Duration is the standard measure of a bond's sensitivity to interest rates. Macaulay duration is the weighted average time, in years, until the bond's cash flows are received, using each payment's present value as the weight. Modified duration turns this into price sensitivity: a bond with a modified duration of 6 loses about 6% of its value if yields rise by 1 percentage point. Duration generally rises with maturity and falls with higher coupons and higher yields; a zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its maturity. Fund managers lengthen portfolio duration when they expect rates to fall and shorten it when they expect rises, and SEBI's categorisation rules, as of 2025, define several Indian debt fund categories by Macaulay duration. A common confusion is treating duration as maturity; another is relying on it alone for large rate moves, where convexity matters.
example: Say a debt fund's bonds have a portfolio modified duration of 4.5. If yields rise by 0.50 percentage points, its bond holdings fall by roughly 4.5 × 0.50% = 2.25%, so a ₹10 lakh investment loses about ₹22,500.
formula: Approximate % price change = -Modified duration × Change in yield

short: The weighted average time, in years, until a bond's cash flows are received, weighting each payment by its present value.
kid: Picture getting small sweets each week and one big cake at the end. If you balanced all those treats on a see-saw by when they arrive, the balancing point sits close to cake day.
detail: Macaulay duration, introduced by economist Frederick Macaulay in 1938, measures the average time to receive a bond's cash flows, where each payment's timing is weighted by its share of the bond's present value. It is expressed in years. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its maturity; a coupon bond's is shorter because some cash arrives earlier. Higher coupons and higher yields shorten it. It is the natural measure for immunisation: a portfolio whose Macaulay duration matches the timing of a future liability is largely protected against small, parallel rate shifts. In India, under SEBI's rules as of 2025, debt fund categories such as low duration and medium duration funds are defined by the portfolio's Macaulay duration. A common confusion is using Macaulay duration directly as price sensitivity; for that, convert it to modified duration.
example: A 2-year ₹1,000 bond with a 10% annual coupon, priced at a 10% yield, pays ₹100 in year 1 and ₹1,100 in year 2. Their present values are ₹90.91 and ₹909.09, adding to ₹1,000, so Macaulay duration = (1 × 90.91 + 2 × 909.09) / 1,000 = 1.91 years.
formula: Macaulay duration = Sum of [t × PV of cash flow at time t] / Bond price

short: The approximate percentage fall in a bond's price for a one percentage point rise in its yield.
kid: Push down a little on one end of a see-saw and the other end moves too. This number tells you how far it moves for a small push.
detail: Modified duration turns Macaulay duration into a direct measure of price sensitivity: Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield per period. If a bond's modified duration is 7, a 1 percentage point rise in yield cuts its price by about 7%, and a 1 point fall raises it by about 7%. Indian debt mutual funds report it in their factsheets alongside yield to maturity, and traders use it to size hedges. Its limits: it assumes cash flows do not change when yields change, so it misleads for bonds with embedded options, where effective duration is used; and as a straight-line estimate it understates price gains and overstates losses for large moves, because of convexity. A common confusion is reading modified duration as a time in years; strictly, it is a percentage sensitivity, even though its value is close to Macaulay duration.
example: The 2-year 10% coupon bond priced at a 10% yield has a Macaulay duration of 1.909 years, so its modified duration is 1.909 / 1.10 = 1.74. If its yield rises to 10.5%, the price is estimated to fall about 1.74 × 0.5% = 0.87%, from ₹1,000 to about ₹991.30; the exact new price is ₹991.38.
formula: Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + y/k), where y is the annual yield and k the number of coupon payments per year
related: Price value of a basis point

short: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to interest rates that allows for its cash flows changing when rates move, as with callable bonds.
kid: Some promises change with the weather, like a friend who returns your umbrella early if the rain stops. This check looks at what happens in both kinds of weather.
detail: Effective duration estimates price sensitivity by repricing the bond with a valuation model after shifting the yield curve up and down by a small amount, rather than using a formula that assumes fixed cash flows. That makes it the right measure for bonds whose cash flows depend on rates: callable and puttable bonds, mortgage-backed securities and floating-rate notes. For a callable bond, falling rates make a call more likely, which caps price gains, so its effective duration is lower than its modified duration. For a bond without options, effective and modified duration are almost the same. Bond index and fund factsheets, especially in the US, often report effective duration. The common confusion is assuming modified duration works for every bond; it ignores embedded options and can badly overstate a callable bond's sensitivity.
example: Say a bond is priced at ₹1,000, and a model values it at ₹1,020 if yields fall 0.5 percentage points and ₹975 if they rise 0.5 points. Effective duration = (1,020 - 975) / (2 × 1,000 × 0.005) = 45 / 10 = 4.5.
formula: Effective duration = (Price if yields fall - Price if yields rise) / (2 × Initial price × Change in yield)

short: A bond or portfolio's price sensitivity to a change in the yield at one specific maturity, with yields at other maturities unchanged.
kid: A piano has many keys. Pressing one key changes only that note, and this number tells you how much your song changes when just that key is pressed.
detail: Ordinary duration assumes yields at every maturity move by the same amount, a parallel shift, but in practice the yield curve twists: short rates may rise while long rates fall. Key rate duration splits sensitivity into pieces by shifting the yield at one key maturity, such as 2, 5, 10 or 30 years, by a small amount and measuring the price change. A portfolio's key rate durations add up to approximately its effective duration. Portfolio managers and bank treasuries use them to see exactly where along the curve they are exposed and to hedge with instruments at the right maturities. Two portfolios with the same total duration can behave very differently if one is concentrated at 5 years and the other is a barbell split between 1 and 30 years. The common confusion is assuming the same total duration means the same risk.
example: Say a ₹100 crore portfolio has key rate durations of 0.5 at 2 years, 1.5 at 5 years and 3.0 at 10 years, adding to 5.0. If only the 10-year yield rises by 0.20 percentage points, the portfolio falls by about 3.0 × 0.20% = 0.6%, or ₹60 lakh.
formula: Key rate duration at maturity k = -(Change in price / Price) / Change in yield at maturity k

short: A measure of how a bond's sensitivity to interest rates itself changes as rates move, capturing the curve in the price-yield relationship.
kid: On a curved slide, you speed up more going down than you slow down climbing the same distance up. Some promises act like that slide: they go up more than they go down.
detail: Duration gives a straight-line estimate of how a bond's price reacts to yield changes, but the true price-yield relationship is curved. Convexity measures that curvature. For an ordinary bond it is positive: when yields fall, the price rises more than duration predicts, and when yields rise, it falls less. Adding a convexity term to the duration estimate makes it accurate for larger moves. Longer maturities, lower coupons and more spread-out cash flows mean more convexity, which investors value, especially when rates are volatile. Callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities can show negative convexity: as yields fall, their prices rise less, or even flatten, because the issuer or borrowers are likely to repay early. A common confusion is that convexity matters only to specialists; it is the reason duration-only estimates understate gains and overstate losses.
example: A bond has a modified duration of 7 and a convexity of 60. For a 1 percentage point rise in yields, duration alone predicts a 7% fall; adding convexity, the estimate is -7 × 0.01 + 0.5 × 60 × 0.01^2 = -6.7%. For a 1 point fall, it is +7.3%.
formula: % price change ≈ -Modified duration × Δy + 0.5 × Convexity × (Δy)^2

term: Price value of a basis point
hl: price value of a basis point
dollar value of a basis point
short: The change in a bond's price, in money terms, when its yield moves by one basis point, which is 0.01 percentage point.
kid: Nudge a toy car with your little finger and see how far it rolls. This number tells you how far your pile of promises moves with the tiniest nudge.
detail: PVBP, also called DV01 or PV01, expresses interest rate risk in currency rather than percentages: how many rupees or dollars a position gains or loses for a one basis point, or 0.01 percentage point, change in yield. It equals modified duration × market value × 0.0001. Traders and bank treasuries use it because it can be added across bonds, swaps and futures, making it easy to set risk limits and size hedges: to hedge a position, take an opposite position with the same PVBP. Conventions vary between desks, and in swap markets PV01 sometimes means the value of a one basis point annuity. The common confusion is mixing up percentage sensitivity, which is duration, with money sensitivity, which is PVBP: a small holding with high duration can have a lower PVBP than a large holding with low duration.
example: Say a bank holds ₹500 crore of government bonds with a modified duration of 6. Its PVBP is ₹500 crore × 6 × 0.0001 = ₹30 lakh, so a 10 basis point rise in yields costs it about ₹3 crore.
formula: PVBP = Modified duration × Market value of position × 0.0001

short: The risk that a change in interest rates reduces the value of an investment, especially bonds, whose prices fall when rates rise.
kid: You have a toy that gives one sweet a day, and then new toys start giving two. Suddenly your toy seems less special, and that chance of it losing its shine is the worry.
detail: Interest rate risk is the possibility that rate changes hurt an investor or institution. For bondholders it is mainly price risk: rising yields push down the prices of existing fixed-coupon bonds, and the effect grows with duration. It hits anyone who must sell before maturity or who values holdings at market prices, such as debt mutual funds, whose NAVs fall when yields jump. For banks it also shows up as a mismatch between the rates on assets and liabilities, managed through asset-liability management; the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank followed heavy losses on long-dated bonds after US rates rose sharply. The risk works both ways: falling rates lift bond prices but create reinvestment risk. A common confusion is thinking government bonds are risk-free in every sense: they carry almost no default risk but plenty of interest rate risk.
example: Say you hold ₹5 lakh in a government bond fund with a modified duration of 8. If yields rise by 0.75 percentage points, the fund's value drops by about 8 × 0.75% = 6%, or ₹30,000, even though no bond has defaulted.
formula: Approximate % price change = -Modified duration × Change in yield

short: The risk that interest received or money from a maturing investment must be reinvested at lower rates than before, reducing overall return.
kid: A helper gives you three sweets a week, and you swap them for more treats. If the swapping gets worse, your pile grows more slowly than you hoped.
detail: Reinvestment risk arises when cash from an investment, such as coupons, a maturing bond or a called bond, has to be put back to work at lower rates. Yield to maturity quietly assumes every coupon is reinvested at that same yield; if rates fall, the realised return comes in below the YTM promised at purchase. The risk is highest for high-coupon bonds, short-term investments that must be rolled over often and callable bonds, which issuers redeem precisely when rates have dropped. It is the mirror image of price risk: falling rates raise bond prices but cut reinvestment income, and rising rates do the reverse, a balance that immunisation strategies exploit. Zero-coupon bonds held to maturity have no reinvestment risk. A familiar example is a retiree whose fixed deposits mature after rates have fallen, leaving less interest income.
example: Say a retiree has ₹20 lakh in a 1-year deposit at 7.5%, earning ₹1.5 lakh. If, at maturity, the best rate available is 6.5%, the same ₹20 lakh earns only ₹1.3 lakh the next year, ₹20,000 less.

short: A bond that pays no regular interest but is sold below its face value and repaid at full face value at maturity.
kid: You give a friend eight marbles today, and she promises to give you ten back next summer. You get nothing in between, just the bigger pile at the end.
detail: A zero-coupon bond makes a single payment, its face value, at maturity. The investor's whole return is the difference between the discounted purchase price and that face value, which compounds at the bond's yield. Treasury bills are short-term zeros, and longer zeros are created by stripping the coupons and principal of government bonds into separate securities, known as STRIPS in both the US and India. Because all the cash comes at the end, a zero's Macaulay duration equals its maturity, so long zeros are very sensitive to rate changes, and there is no reinvestment risk if held to maturity. Pension funds and insurers use them to match known future payouts. A common confusion is thinking a zero earns no interest; it does, but the interest is built into the price gain, and tax rules may treat that accrued gain as income each year.
example: A 5-year zero-coupon bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000, priced at an 8% annual yield, costs ₹1,00,000 / 1.08^5 = ₹68,058. The investor receives nothing until year 5, then ₹1,00,000, a gain of ₹31,942.
formula: Price = Face value / (1 + y)^n

short: A short-term government borrowing instrument, lasting a year or less, sold below face value and repaid at full face value.
kid: You lend the town council ninety-eight coins, and three months later it gives you back a hundred. The council always keeps its promises, so this is about the safest lending there is.
detail: A treasury bill is a zero-coupon money market instrument issued by a central government to manage short-term cash needs. It pays no coupon; investors buy it at a discount and receive face value at maturity, and the difference is their return. In India, the RBI auctions T-bills for the central government in 91-day, 182-day and 364-day tenors, usually every week; US T-bills run from a few weeks to 52 weeks. Being short-dated and backed by the sovereign, they are the closest thing to a risk-free asset, so their yields anchor short-term rates. Banks, money market funds and companies hold them, and individuals can buy them through RBI Retail Direct. A common confusion is computing the return as the discount over face value; the yield should be measured on the price actually paid.
example: A 91-day T-bill with a face value of ₹100 is bought for ₹98.25. The gain is ₹1.75, so the annualised yield is (1.75 / 98.25) × (365 / 91) = about 7.14%.
formula: Yield = [(Face value - Price) / Price] × (365 / Days to maturity)

short: A very short-term Indian government bill, maturing in under 91 days, used to cover temporary gaps between government spending and receipts.
kid: Sometimes a grown-up runs short of coins for a few days before payday and borrows from a neighbour, then pays it back quickly. This is that kind of quick, tiny borrowing.
detail: Cash management bills were introduced by the Government of India, in consultation with the RBI, to meet temporary mismatches between the government's spending and its receipts, such as the weeks before advance tax collections arrive. They work like treasury bills: zero-coupon, issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, but with maturities of less than 91 days, set to fit the specific gap. Unlike regular T-bills, CMBs are not on a fixed calendar; the RBI announces them as needed. Banks can count them towards their statutory liquidity ratio, and banks, mutual funds and others bid in the auctions. The US Treasury also issues cash management bills for short funding needs. A common confusion is reading CMB issuance as a sign of fiscal stress; it is routine cash management, not extra long-term borrowing.
example: Say the RBI auctions a 35-day CMB with a face value of ₹100 at a price of ₹99.40. The investor earns ₹0.60, an annualised yield of (0.60 / 99.40) × (365 / 35) = about 6.29%.
formula: Yield = [(Face value - Price) / Price] × (365 / Days to maturity)

short: A tradable debt instrument issued by a central or state government; in India, the term often means the government's longer-dated bonds.
kid: When the whole country needs to build roads and schools, it borrows from people and promises to pay them back with a little extra. It is the most trusted promise in the land.
detail: In India, government securities, or G-secs, are instruments issued by the central government or state governments: treasury bills, cash management bills, dated securities and state development loans. Dated securities are the long-term bonds, with maturities from a few years to as long as 50 years, usually paying fixed semi-annual coupons. The RBI runs the auctions and keeps the register; trading happens mainly on its NDS-OM platform, and individuals can buy through RBI Retail Direct or stock exchanges. Because the central government can always meet rupee obligations, its securities carry virtually no default risk and anchor all other rupee interest rates. Banks hold them to meet the statutory liquidity ratio, and since 2024 eligible G-secs have entered global indices such as JP Morgan's GBI-EM government bond index. A common confusion is that no default risk means no losses: G-sec prices still fall when yields rise.
example: Say you buy ₹1 lakh face value of a 7% central government dated security at ₹100 per ₹100 of face value. You receive ₹3,500 every six months, ₹7,000 a year, and ₹1 lakh at maturity.

short: A bond issued by an Indian state government to borrow from the market, auctioned on its behalf by the Reserve Bank of India.
kid: Your neighbourhood wants a new playground, so it borrows coins from families nearby and promises to pay them back with a little extra each year.
detail: State development loans are dated securities issued by Indian state governments to fund their budget deficits. The RBI, as the states' debt manager, auctions them, usually every week, following a quarterly calendar of indicative amounts. SDLs typically pay semi-annual coupons, count towards banks' statutory liquidity ratio and trade on NDS-OM like central government securities. No state has defaulted on its market borrowings, yet SDLs trade at a yield spread over central G-secs of similar maturity, reflecting lower liquidity and differences in states' finances, though spreads vary less across states than their finances would suggest, partly because the RBI services the debt from states' accounts. Together, states are among the largest borrowers in the Indian bond market. The common confusion is treating SDLs as central government bonds: each is a separate obligation of the issuing state.
example: Say a state auctions a 10-year SDL at a 7.45% cut-off yield when a comparable central G-sec yields 7.10%. The spread is 0.35 percentage points, or 35 basis points, so on ₹1,000 crore the state pays about ₹3.5 crore more interest a year than the centre would.

short: Debt issued by the US federal government, including bills, notes and bonds, widely treated as the world's benchmark safe asset.
kid: The biggest, most trusted family in town borrows from everyone and always pays back. People all over the world keep their savings with this family because it feels so safe.
detail: US Treasury securities are issued by the US Department of the Treasury to fund the federal government. Bills mature in a year or less and pay no coupon; notes run from 2 to 10 years and bonds for 20 or 30 years, both paying semi-annual coupons; TIPS protect against inflation, and floating rate notes reset with bill rates. The Treasury market is the largest and most liquid bond market in the world, and the 10-year Treasury yield is the reference rate for global borrowing costs, US mortgages and equity valuations. Central banks, including the RBI, hold Treasuries in their reserves, and moves in US yields ripple through to Indian bond yields, the rupee and foreign portfolio flows. A common confusion is between US Treasuries and treasury bills elsewhere, such as India's T-bills; another is assuming safe from default means safe from price falls.
example: A 10-year Treasury note with $1,000 face value and a 4% coupon pays $20 every six months, $40 a year. If its price falls to $960, a buyer still receives the $20 payments and $1,000 at maturity, so their yield is higher than 4%.

short: A bond issued by the UK government, the British counterpart of US Treasuries or Indian government securities.
kid: Long ago, the papers Britain gave people when it borrowed from them had shiny gold edges. The name stuck, so these promises are still named after gold.
detail: Gilts are sterling bonds issued by HM Treasury and managed by the UK Debt Management Office. The name comes from the gilded edges of the original paper certificates, a sign of their safety. Conventional gilts pay a fixed coupon every six months and repay face value at maturity, while index-linked gilts adjust both coupon and principal for UK inflation. UK pension funds are major holders, which is why the September 2022 mini-budget, which sent gilt yields sharply higher, triggered collateral calls on pension funds' liability-driven investment strategies and led the Bank of England to step in with emergency gilt purchases. In India, the word gilt is used loosely for government securities, as in gilt mutual funds. A common confusion: Premium Bonds and other National Savings products are not gilts.
example: Say a conventional gilt has £100 face value and a 4% coupon. It pays £2 every six months, and if bought at £95, the buyer also gains £5 when it repays £100 at maturity.

short: A long-term bond issued by the German federal government, used as the benchmark safe asset for the euro area.
kid: In a big group of friends who use the same kind of coins, one friend is known for always being careful with money. When that friend borrows, everyone is sure they will be paid back.
detail: Bund is short for Bundesanleihe, the long-dated bonds of up to 30 years issued by the Federal Republic of Germany; shorter federal debt includes the 5-year Bobl and the 2-year Schatz. Because Germany has a strong fiscal record and the euro area lacks a single, deep common government bond, the 10-year Bund yield serves as the euro area's risk-free benchmark, much as the 10-year Treasury does for the dollar. Other euro countries' borrowing costs are often quoted as a spread over Bunds, so a widening Italy-Bund spread is read as rising stress. Bund futures traded on Eurex are among the world's most active interest rate futures. The 10-year Bund yield was negative for long stretches between 2016 and 2022, meaning investors effectively paid to lend to Germany. A common confusion is calling every German bond a Bund: the term means the federal government's long-dated securities.
example: Say the 10-year Bund yields 2.5% and the 10-year Italian government bond yields 3.7%. The Italy-Bund spread is then 1.2 percentage points, or 120 basis points.

short: A bond issued by the government of Japan, which runs one of the largest government bond markets in the world.
kid: Japan borrows a huge pile of coins, mostly from its own people and its own big coin-keeper, and gives them promises to pay back later with a little extra.
detail: JGBs are yen bonds issued by Japan's Ministry of Finance, ranging from short-term bills to 40-year bonds, plus inflation-indexed issues. Japan's government debt is the highest among major economies relative to GDP, yet borrowing costs stayed extremely low for decades because the debt is mostly held at home and the Bank of Japan bought huge amounts. From 2016 the BOJ ran yield curve control, holding the 10-year JGB yield near 0%, and it ended that policy, along with negative interest rates, in 2024. Because Japanese yields were so low for so long, investors borrowed cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad, the yen carry trade, so shifts in JGB yields can move global bond markets and currencies. A common confusion is treating high debt as an imminent default risk: Japan borrows in its own currency, mostly from domestic savers and institutions.
example: Say a 10-year JGB with ¥1,000,000 face value pays a 1% coupon. It pays ¥5,000 every six months, ¥10,000 a year, so ten years of coupons total ¥100,000, plus ¥1,000,000 at maturity.

short: A bond issued by a company to borrow from investors, usually paying a higher yield than government bonds because the company could fail to pay.
kid: A lemonade stand wants a bigger table, so it borrows coins from friends and promises to pay back a little extra. A stand can have a bad summer, so it promises a bigger thank-you than the town council would.
detail: Companies issue corporate bonds to fund expansion, refinance loans or manage working capital, as an alternative to bank borrowing or issuing shares. Investors receive coupons and principal, but unlike government bonds these depend on the company's ability to pay, so they carry credit risk. Rating agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA and CARE in India, or S&P and Moody's globally, grade issuers, and lower ratings demand higher yields; the gap over a government bond of similar maturity is the credit spread. In India most corporate bonds are privately placed with institutions and listed on NSE or BSE, and they are often called debentures or NCDs. Highly rated issuers such as banks, NBFCs and public sector companies dominate the market. Bondholders rank ahead of shareholders in a liquidation. A common confusion is that a high coupon means a better bond; it usually signals a higher risk of default.
example: Say ABC Ltd, rated AA, issues 5-year bonds at an 8.4% yield when a 5-year G-sec yields 7.0%. Its credit spread is 1.4 percentage points, so on ₹500 crore it pays ₹7 crore a year more in interest than the government would.
formula: Credit spread = Corporate bond yield - Government bond yield of similar maturity

short: A debt instrument a company issues to borrow money from the public or institutions, acknowledging the debt and promising interest and repayment.
kid: When a shop borrows coins from you, it gives you a signed note saying it owes you and will pay back with a little extra. That signed note is what this is.
detail: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of debt issued by a company, carrying a fixed or floating rate of interest and a repayment date. In India, the Companies Act, 2013 uses debenture as the umbrella term for corporate bonds, and debentures may be secured by a charge on company assets, held through a debenture trustee, or unsecured. They can be non-convertible, partly convertible or fully convertible into shares. Debenture holders are creditors with no voting rights, paid before shareholders if the company is wound up. Usage differs across countries: in the US, a debenture usually means an unsecured bond backed only by the issuer's general credit, while in the UK and India it is often secured. The common confusion is assuming a debenture is always secured, or always unsecured; only its terms tell you which.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues 10,000 secured debentures of ₹1,000 each at 9% annual interest, raising ₹1 crore. It pays ₹9 lakh of interest a year and must repay ₹1 crore at maturity.

short: A debenture that can never be converted into the company's shares, paying only interest and repaying its principal at maturity.
kid: You lend a shop ten coins and it promises to pay you back with a little extra. It will never give you a piece of the shop instead, only coins.
detail: A non-convertible debenture is a plain company debt instrument: fixed or floating interest, repayment on a set date and no option to turn it into shares. Because there is no equity upside, NCDs usually pay more interest than convertible debentures from the same issuer. In India, companies, especially NBFCs and housing finance companies, raise money through NCDs placed privately with institutions and through public NCD issues aimed at retail investors, which list on NSE or BSE and, under SEBI rules as of 2025, must carry a credit rating. NCDs can be secured or unsecured, and some offer a cumulative option that pays all interest at maturity. Listed NCDs can be sold before maturity, though trading is often thin. A common confusion is equating NCDs with bank fixed deposits: NCDs have no deposit insurance, and their safety depends entirely on the issuer.
example: Say ABC Finance Ltd offers a 3-year NCD with ₹1,000 face value at 9.5% interest paid annually. An investor buying 100 NCDs pays ₹1 lakh, receives ₹9,500 a year and gets ₹1 lakh back at the end, for total interest of ₹28,500.

short: A bond the holder can exchange for a set number of the issuing company's shares, combining steady interest with a chance to share in gains.
kid: You lend a lemonade stand some coins. Later you can choose: get your coins back, or swap them for a small piece of the stand if it has become a big success.
detail: A convertible bond pays interest like an ordinary bond but gives the holder the right to convert it into a fixed number of the issuer's shares, the conversion ratio, usually at a conversion price above the share price at issue. If the shares rise well above the conversion price, the bond behaves like equity; if they languish, it behaves like a bond and the holder still receives coupons and principal. In return for this built-in equity option, investors accept a lower coupon, so issuers, often growth companies, borrow cheaply. In India, compulsorily convertible debentures (CCDs) must convert into shares and are treated as equity under India's foreign investment rules as of 2025, while optionally convertible debentures leave the choice to the holder. A common confusion is ignoring dilution: conversion increases the share count, which existing shareholders must account for.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues a ₹1,000 convertible bond with a 3% coupon, convertible into 20 shares, a conversion price of ₹50. If the share price rises to ₹80, converting gives shares worth 20 × ₹80 = ₹1,600; if it stays at ₹40, the holder keeps the bond and gets ₹1,000 back.
formula: Conversion ratio = Face value / Conversion price; Conversion value = Conversion ratio × Current share price

short: A convertible bond issued by a company in a foreign currency, such as dollars, to overseas investors and convertible into its shares.
kid: A lemonade stand borrows coins from children in another country, in their kind of coins. Later, those children can swap the loan for a piece of the stand instead of getting coins back.
detail: An FCCB is a bond issued in a currency other than the issuer's home currency, typically US dollars, that pays a low coupon and can be converted into the issuer's equity shares at a preset price. Indian companies used FCCBs heavily in the mid-2000s to raise cheap foreign money, since the conversion option let them pay low or even zero coupons. In India, as of 2025, issuance is governed by a 1993 FCCB scheme together with FEMA rules on external commercial borrowings. The risks are twofold: if the share price falls, holders do not convert and the company must repay in foreign currency, and if the rupee weakens, that repayment costs more in rupees. After the 2008 crash, many Indian FCCB issuers struggled to repay. A common confusion is treating FCCBs as equity: until converted, they are foreign-currency debt.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues a $10 million FCCB when $1 = ₹75, raising ₹75 crore, convertible at ₹500 per share. If the shares stay below ₹500 and the rupee weakens to ₹85 per dollar, repaying $10 million costs ₹85 crore.

short: A bond the issuer can repay before maturity, on set dates and at a set price, usually to refinance at lower interest rates.
kid: You lend a friend ten sweets and she gives you one extra every week. But she is allowed to hand the ten back early, and she will if someone else lends to her more cheaply, so your extras stop.
detail: A callable bond includes a call provision that lets the issuer redeem it before maturity at a stated call price, often face value or a small premium, usually after an initial protection period. Issuers call bonds when interest rates fall or their credit improves, so they can refinance more cheaply. That timing hurts investors: they get cash back just when reinvestment rates are low, and the bond's price gains are capped near the call price, a pattern called negative convexity. To compensate, callable bonds pay higher yields than similar non-callable ones, and investors judge them by yield to worst. Many US corporate and municipal bonds are callable, and in India banks' perpetual Additional Tier 1 bonds carry call options that markets expect banks to exercise. The common confusion is assuming a call will happen on the first date; it is always the issuer's choice.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues a 10-year ₹1,000 bond with a 9% coupon, callable at ₹1,000 after 3 years. If yields on similar bonds fall to 7% by then, ABC can call the bond and borrow again at 7%, saving ₹20 a year per bond, while the investor must reinvest at the lower rate.

short: A bond that lets the holder demand early repayment from the issuer on set dates, usually at its face value.
kid: You lend a friend your skateboard for a year, but you are allowed to ask for it back early. If a better deal comes along, you can take it back and use it elsewhere.
detail: A puttable bond gives the investor, not the issuer, the right to sell the bond back to the issuer at a set put price, typically face value, on specified dates before maturity. Holders exercise the put when interest rates have risen, so they can reinvest at higher yields, or when the issuer's credit is weakening and they want their money back. Because this protects investors, puttable bonds pay lower yields than otherwise identical plain bonds, and their prices fall less when rates rise, since the put sets a floor near the put price. In India, some corporate bonds and debentures carry put and call options exercisable on the same date. A common confusion is mixing up the two: a call option benefits the issuer, while a put option benefits the holder.
example: Say you hold a 10-year ₹1,000 bond of ABC Ltd with a 7% coupon, puttable at ₹1,000 after 4 years. If yields on similar bonds rise to 9% by then, you put it back, receive ₹1,000 and reinvest at 9%, earning ₹90 a year instead of ₹70.

short: A right built into a bond's terms, such as a call, put or conversion feature, that cannot be traded separately from the bond.
kid: Some toys come with a secret button inside, like a car that can turn into a robot. You cannot get the button on its own; it only comes with that toy.
detail: An embedded option is a feature within a bond that gives the issuer or the holder a right that changes the bond's cash flows. Issuer options include calls, sinking-fund provisions and the prepayment rights inside mortgage-backed securities; holder options include puts, conversion into shares and extension rights. The bond's value is the value of an otherwise identical straight bond, plus any option held by the investor or minus any option held by the issuer. Because the cash flows depend on future rates or share prices, standard yield to maturity and modified duration mislead, so analysts use option-adjusted spread, effective duration and yield to worst, valuing the options with binomial tree or Monte Carlo models. A common confusion is treating the bond and its option as separable; unlike a listed option, an embedded option cannot be sold on its own and lives and dies with the bond.
example: Say an otherwise identical straight bond is worth ₹1,040 and the issuer's call option is worth ₹25. The callable bond is worth ₹1,040 - ₹25 = ₹1,015. If instead the holder had a put worth ₹15, the puttable bond would be worth ₹1,040 + ₹15 = ₹1,055.
formula: Callable bond value = Straight bond value - Call option value; Puttable bond value = Straight bond value + Put option value
